stem:
A woman at 29+2 weeks whose membranes ruptured three days ago is now contracting regularly, and the cervix is 5 cm dilated. She completed a course of betamethasone yesterday, intravenous benzylpenicillin has been started, and her blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg with no proteinuria. Birth is expected within hours and the neonatal team has been called.

Which further treatment should the obstetric registrar start?

options.label: A
options.text: Nifedipine to delay birth long enough for a repeat steroid course
options.explanation: Corticosteroids are already complete, tocolysis is not used once labour is established after membrane rupture, and it would not protect the brain.

options.label: B
options.text: Magnesium sulfate if severe hypertension or proteinuria develops later
options.explanation: Here magnesium is given for fetal neuroprotection, not to prevent eclampsia, so a normal blood pressure does not remove the indication.

options.label: C
options.text: Amoxicillin–clavulanate, to broaden cover now that labour has begun
options.explanation: Amoxicillin–clavulanate is avoided after preterm membrane rupture because of its link with necrotising enterocolitis, and benzylpenicillin already covers GBS.

options.label: D
options.text: A second course of betamethasone, since birth is now imminent
options.explanation: Her course finished yesterday; a repeat dose is considered only after at least seven days.

options.label: E
options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate, loading dose then infusion until birth
options.explanation: Magnesium sulfate before birth under 30 weeks reduces the risk of cerebral palsy. It is indicated when birth is expected within 24 hours, whatever her blood pressure.

context: Give magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection when birth before 30 weeks is expected within 24 hours, even in a normotensive woman.
